graphNodes.title: Basic Safety
graphNodes.summary: Defensive play techniques in billiards that make it difficult for opponents to score. Covers hook, side safety, and long safety strategies.
graphNodes.description: Basic safety play involves controlling cue ball position and creating difficult scenarios for opponents. Key techniques include keeping opponent balls far from pockets, controlling the cue ball to avoid giving opportunities, and creating challenging angles.

graphNodes.title: Closed Bridge
graphNodes.summary: A bridge technique where the index finger wraps around the thumb, creating a enclosed loop for more precise cue control.
graphNodes.description: Closed bridge provides tighter control compared to open bridge, especially for soft shots. The technique involves placing the hand like an open bridge, then folding the index finger down to touch the thumb, creating a closed loop around the cue.

graphNodes.title: Cut Shots
graphNodes.summary: Shots where the cue ball travels at an angle to the target ball, requiring adjustment of aim point opposite to the cut angle.
graphNodes.description: Cut shots are fundamental aiming techniques where the cue ball does not travel straight to the target ball but at an angle. Cut angles range from thin cuts (1-30 degrees) to thick cuts (60-90 degrees), with accuracy requirements increasing with angle size.

graphNodes.title: Draw Shot
graphNodes.summary: Shot that applies backspin to the cue ball, causing it to reverse direction after hitting the target ball.
graphNodes.description: Draw shot applies backspin to the cue ball by striking below center (1/4 to 1/2 of ball height). The cue ball travels forward, and after impact with the target ball, reverses direction. Mastery levels progress from 20-30cm draw to full table draws.

graphNodes.title: Follow Shot
graphNodes.summary: Shot that applies topspin to the cue ball, causing it to continue in the same direction as the target ball after impact.
graphNodes.description: Follow shot applies topspin by striking above center of the cue ball (1/4 to 1/2 above center). Requires 20-30% more power than normal shots and a long follow-through to overcome backspin from table cloth friction.

graphNodes.title: Ghost Ball Method
graphNodes.summary: Aiming technique where players visualize an imaginary cue ball at the contact point needed for the shot.
graphNodes.description: Ghost ball is the most popular aiming method in billiards. Players imagine a ghost ball at the exact position where the cue ball needs to be for the target ball to go into the pocket. The aim point is determined by the contact point between the target ball and the ghost ball.

graphNodes.title: Open Bridge
graphNodes.summary: The most common bridge technique where the index finger creates a loop around the cue with thumb support.
graphNodes.description: Open bridge is the standard and easiest bridge technique. The hand is placed on the table with the thumb pointing forward, index finger wrapped to create a loop, and other fingers flat on the table. The gap between thumb and index finger guides the cue.

graphNodes.title: Position Play
graphNodes.summary: Advanced skill of controlling cue ball position to set up for the next shot, distinguishing good players from great ones.
graphNodes.description: Position play is the ability to control where the cue ball ends up after a shot, ideally in a favorable position for the next ball. Key principles include planning ahead, leaving options, and controlling pace. Techniques involve speed control, spin application, and utilizing natural angles.
